extraction_notes.note: The introduction's dependency diagram among the main theorems is omitted in the prepared source ('[omitted: a diagram ...]'), so no node or edge is taken from it.
Remark 2.24 states a cited fact (columns of D-matrices are d-vectors, FZ3 (7.7)); retyped as an external theorem rather than remark.

Lemma A.4 is justified twice: first by a one-sentence appeal to the length-function result of Geroldinger-Halter-Koch, then by a full proof environment separated from the lemma by that prose; the prose justification is marked as the alternative proof and both proves edges were added by hand.

The definition of lambda_t in the appendix is embedded in an argument (factoriality of L(t,inv), well-definedness of the number of irreducible factors); the whole paragraph is kept as one definition node.

Introduction summaries of the main theorems (with \ref pointers) and the informal intro descriptions of cluster algebras are not separate nodes; verbatim intro copies of definitions/results are recorded in also_stated_at.
Theorem 2.35 part (i) is cited from GLS13 and part (ii) is the paper's transfer of the same argument to U; marked external as a whole.

nodes.name: Notation F_{k;t}
nodes.statement: When $B$ and $t_0$ are clear, we simply write $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$ as $F_{k;t}$.
nodes.section: Application to $F$-polynomials

nodes.name: Positivity and constant term of F-polynomials
nodes.statement: It is known that $F$-polynomials enjoy many nice properties, for example, they have positive coefficients and constant term $1$.
nodes.section: Application to $F$-polynomials
conclusions: they have positive coefficients and constant term $1$
nodes.statement_short: F-polynomials have positive coefficients and constant term 1.

nodes.name: Ground ring assumption
nodes.statement:
Throughout this article,   $\mathbb K$ is assumed to be a factorial domain of characteristic $0$ (e.g., $\mathbb K=\mathbb Z, \mathbb Q, \mathbb R, \mathbb C$)
and all upper cluster algebras are considered as algebras over $\mathbb {KP}$, where $\mathbb P$ is some abelian multiplicative group and $\mathbb{KP}$ the corresponding group ring.
nodes.section: 1.4 Convention and assumption
nodes.statement_short: K is a factorial domain of characteristic 0; upper cluster algebras are KP-algebras for an abelian group P.

nodes.name: Exchange binomials are not invertible
nodes.statement: We always assume that the {\em exchange binomials} of upper cluster algebras in this article are {\em not invertible in $\mathbb {KP}$}.
nodes.section: 1.4 Convention and assumption

nodes.name: Freezing trivial exchange relations
nodes.statement: Note that when $\mathbb K=\mathbb Z$, this condition is always satisfied. When $\mathbb K$ is a field and we have a {\em trivial exchange relation} $$A_{k}A_k^\prime=P_k\in(\mathbb{KP})^\times$$ in an upper cluster algebra $\mathcal U$,  we can always freeze the cluster variable $A_k$ and consider the upper cluster algebra $\mathcal U^\dag$ with smaller rank over $\mathbb {KP}^\dag=\mathbb {KP}[A_k^\pm]$. Note that $\mathcal U^\dag$ and $\mathcal U$ are isomorphic as $\mathbb K$-algebras.
nodes.section: 1.4 Convention and assumption
nodes.statement_short: If K is a field and an exchange relation is trivial, the variable can be frozen to give an isomorphic upper cluster algebra of smaller rank.

nodes.name: Skew-symmetrizable matrix
nodes.statement: An $n\times n$ integer matrix $B$ is said to be {\em  skew-symmetrizable} if there is an integer diagonal matrix $S$ with strictly positive diagonal entries such that $SB$ is skew-symmetric.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
differentia: there is an integer diagonal matrix $S$ with strictly positive diagonal entries such that $SB$ is skew-symmetric

nodes.name: Skew-symmetrizer
nodes.statement: Such an $S$ is said to be a {\em  skew-symmetrizer} of $B$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Matrix mutation
nodes.statement: Let $\widetilde B=\begin{pmatrix}B_{n\times n}\\C_{m\times n}\end{pmatrix}=(b_{ij})$ be an $(n+m)\times n$ integer matrix with $B$ skew-symmetrizable. The mutation $\mu_k(\widetilde B)$ of $\widetilde B$ at $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is the new matrix $\mu_k(\widetilde B)=\widetilde B^\prime= \begin{pmatrix}B_{n\times n}^\prime\\C_{m\times n}^\prime\end{pmatrix}=(b_{ij}^\prime)$ given by \begin{eqnarray} b_{ij}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}-b_{ij}~,&\text{if } i=k\text{ or } j=k;\\ b_{ij}+{\rm sgn}(b_{ik}){\rm max}(b_{ik}b_{kj},0)~,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: Mutation of an extended skew-symmetrizable matrix at k: negate row/column k, adjust other entries by sgn(b_ik)max(b_ik b_kj,0).

nodes.name: Matrix mutation is an involution preserving skew-symmetrizability
nodes.statement: It is not hard to check that the submatrix $B^\prime$ of $\widetilde B^\prime$ is still skew-symmetrizable with the same skew-symmetrizer as $B$ and that $\mu_k$ is an involution.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
conclusions: the submatrix $B^\prime$ of $\widetilde B^\prime$ is still skew-symmetrizable with the same skew-symmetrizer as $B$

nodes.name: Mutation preserves rank
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Lemma 3.2]{BFZ}{\rm ).} Matrix mutations preserve the rank of $\widetilde B$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
conclusions: Matrix mutations preserve the rank of $\widetilde B$.
nodes.label: prorank

nodes.name: Semifield
nodes.statement: Recall that $(\mathbb P, \oplus, \cdot)$ is a {\em semifield} if $(\mathbb P,  \cdot)$ is an abelian multiplicative group endowed with a binary operation of auxiliary addition $\oplus$ which is commutative, associative and satisfies that the multiplication  distributes over the auxiliary addition.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
differentia: endowed with a binary operation of auxiliary addition $\oplus$ which is commutative, associative and satisfies that the multiplication  distributes over the auxiliary addition

nodes.name: Tropical semifield
nodes.statement:
The {\em tropical semifield} $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is the free (multiplicative) abelian group generated by $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$
with auxiliary addition $\oplus$ defined by
$$\prod\limits_{i}Z_i^{a_i}\oplus\prod\limits_{i}Z_i^{b_i}=\prod\limits_{i}Z_i^{{\rm min}(a_i,b_i)}.$$
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: Trop(Z_1..Z_m): free abelian group on Z_i with auxiliary addition = componentwise min of exponents.

nodes.name: Subtraction-free rational functions
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbb Q_{\rm sf}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ be the set of all non-zero rational functions in
$m$ independent variables $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$, which can be written as subtraction-free rational expressions in
$Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Universal semifield
nodes.statement:
The set $\mathbb Q_{\rm sf}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$  is a semifield
with respect to the usual operations of multiplication and addition. It is called an {\em universal semifield}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: X-seed and cluster Poisson seed
nodes.statement: (i) A {\em (labeled) $\mathscr X$-seed} over a semifield $\mathbb P$ is a pair $(B,X)$, where \begin{itemize} \item $B=(b_{ij})$ is an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable integer matrix, called an {\em exchange matrix }; \item $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is an $n$-tuple of elements in $\mathbb P$. We call $X$ the {\em $\mathscr X$-cluster} and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ the {\em $\mathscr X$-variables} of $(B,X)$. \end{itemize} (ii) Let $(B,X)$ be an $\mathscr X$-seed over a semifield $\mathbb P$. If $\mathbb P=\mathbb Q_{\rm sf}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$, we call $(B,X)$ a {\em cluster Poisson seed}, $X$ the {\em Poisson cluster}, and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ the {\em cluster Poisson variables} of $(B,X)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: An X-seed is a pair (B,X) of a skew-symmetrizable matrix and an n-tuple in a semifield; over the universal semifield it is a cluster Poisson seed.

nodes.name: Ambient field
nodes.statement: We take the ambient field $\mathcal F$  to be the field of rational functions in $n$ independent variables with coefficients in $\mathbb {KP}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: A-seed
nodes.statement: A {\em (labeled) $\mathscr A$-seed} over $\mathbb P$ is a triple $(B, X, A)$, where \begin{itemize} \item $(B, X)$ forms an $\mathscr X$-seed over $\mathbb P$; \item $A=(A_1,\dots, A_n)$ is an $n$-tuple such that $\{A_1,\dots, A_n\}$ is a free generating set of $\mathcal F$ over $\mathbb{KP}$. We call $A$ the {\em cluster} and $A_1,\dots,A_n$ the {\em cluster variables} of $(B, X, A)$; \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: An A-seed is a triple (B,X,A) with (B,X) an X-seed and A a free generating set of the ambient field.

nodes.name: X-seed mutation and X-exchange pair
nodes.statement: Let $(B,X)$ be an $\mathscr X$-seed over $\mathbb P$. Define the {\em $\mathscr X$-seed mutation} of $(B,X)$ at $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ as a new pair $\mu_k(B,X)=(B^\prime, X^{\prime})$, where $B^\prime=\mu_k(B)$ and $X^\prime=(X_1^\prime,\ldots,X_n^\prime)$ is given by \begin{eqnarray} X_i^{\prime}=\begin{cases} X_k^{-1}~,&\text{if } i=k;\\ X_iX_k^{{\rm max}(b_{ki},0)}(1\bigoplus X_k)^{-b_{ki}}~,&\text{if }i\neq k. \end{cases}\nonumber \end{eqnarray} In this case, $(X_k,X_k^\prime)$ is called an {\em $\mathscr X$-exchange pair}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: Mutation of an X-seed at k: X_k -> X_k^{-1}, other X_i multiplied by X_k^{max(b_ki,0)}(1+X_k)^{-b_ki}.

nodes.name: A-seed mutation, A-exchange pair and exchange binomial
nodes.statement: Let $(B,X, A)$ be an $\mathscr A$-seed over $\mathbb P$. Define the {\em mutation} of $(B,X, A)$ at $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ as a new triple $\mu_k(B,X, A)=(B^\prime,X^\prime, A^\prime)$, where $(B^\prime,X^\prime)=\mu_k(B,X)$ and $A^\prime=(A_1^\prime,\ldots,A_n^\prime)$ is given by $$A_i^{\prime}=\begin{cases}A_i,&\text{if }i\neq k;\\ A_k^{-1}(\frac{X_k}{1\oplus X_k}\prod\limits_{b_{jk}>0}A_j^{b_{jk}}+\frac{1}{1\oplus X_k}\prod\limits_{b_{jk}<0}A_j^{-b_{jk}}),&\text{if }i=k.\end{cases}$$ In this case, $(A_k,A_{k}^\prime)$ is called an {\em $\mathscr A$-exchange pair}. The binomial $$\frac{X_k}{1\oplus X_k}\prod\limits_{b_{jk}>0}A_j^{b_{jk}}+\frac{1}{1\oplus X_k}\prod\limits_{b_{jk}<0}A_j^{-b_{jk}}$$ is called the $k$-th {\em exchange binomial} of $(B,X, A)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: Mutation of an A-seed at k replaces A_k by A_k^{-1} times the k-th exchange binomial; (A_k,A_k') is an A-exchange pair.

nodes.name: Seed mutation is an involution
nodes.statement: It is not hard to check that each mutation $\mu_k$ maps a seed ($\mathscr X$-seed or cluster Poisson seed or $\mathscr A$-seed) to a new seed of the same type and that $\mu_k$ is an involution.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
conclusions: each mutation $\mu_k$ maps a seed ($\mathscr X$-seed or cluster Poisson seed or $\mathscr A$-seed) to a new seed of the same type

nodes.name: n-regular tree
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb T_n$ be the  $n$-regular tree. Let us label the edges of $\mathbb T_n$ by  $1,\dots,n$ such that the $n$  different edges adjacent to the same vertex of $\mathbb T_n$ receive different labels.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Seed pattern
nodes.statement: A {\em seed pattern} $\mathcal S$ over $\mathbb P$ is an assignment of a seed $\Sigma_t$ ($\mathscr X$-seed or cluster Poisson seed or $\mathscr A$-seed) to every vertex $t$ of the $n$-regular tree $\mathbb T_n$ such that $\Sigma_{t^\prime}=\mu_k(\Sigma_t)$ for any edge $t^{~\underline{\quad k \quad}}~ t^{\prime}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Initial seed
nodes.statement: We often fix a vertex $t_0\in\mathbb T_n$ as the rooted vertex of $\mathbb T_n$. For a seed pattern, the seed at the rooted vertex $t_0$ is called the {\em initial seed}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Seed notation
nodes.statement: We always write $B_t=(b_{ij}^t)$, $X_t=(X_{1;t},\ldots,X_{n;t})$ and $A_t=(A_{1;t},\ldots,A_{n;t})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Seed identified with vertex
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we will also use $t$ to denote the seed at $t\in\mathbb T_n$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Equivalent seeds
nodes.statement: Two (labeled) seeds are {\em equivalent} if they are the same up to relabeling.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Exchange graph
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal S$ be a seed pattern. The {\em exchange graph} ${\bf EG}(\mathcal S)$ of $\mathcal S$ is a graph whose vertices are in bijection with the seeds (up to equivalence) of $\mathcal S$ and whose edges correspond to the seed mutations.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
differentia: vertices are in bijection with the seeds (up to equivalence) of $\mathcal S$
edges correspond to the seed mutations

nodes.name: Hat-X seed pattern
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Proposition 3.9]{FZ3}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal S$ be an $\mathscr A$-seed pattern. For each $\mathscr A$-seed $t=(B_t,X_t,A_t)$, let $\widehat X_{t}=(\widehat X_{1;t},\ldots,\widehat X_{n;t})$ be the $n$-tuple of elements in $\mathcal F$ given by $$\widehat X_{j; t}:=X_{j;t}\prod\limits_{i=1}^nA_{i;t}^{b_{ij}^{t}}.$$ Then $\widehat {\mathcal S}=\{(B_{t},\widehat X_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb T_n}$ forms an $\mathscr X$-seed pattern.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal S$ be an $\mathscr A$-seed pattern.
conclusions: Then $\widehat {\mathcal S}=\{(B_{t},\widehat X_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb T_n}$ forms an  $\mathscr X$-seed pattern.
nodes.statement_short: The elements hat X_j = X_j prod A_i^{b_ij} of an A-seed pattern form an X-seed pattern.
nodes.label: proxp

nodes.name: Geometric type
nodes.statement: A seed pattern  $\mathcal S$  over  $\mathbb P$ is said to be of {\em geometric type}, if $\mathbb P$ is a tropical semifield, say $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Principal coefficients
nodes.statement: A seed pattern  $\mathcal S$  over  $\mathbb P$ is said to be with {\em principal coefficients} at $t_0$, if $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ and $X_{i;t_0}=Z_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Universal coefficient semifield
nodes.statement: A seed pattern  $\mathcal S$ over  $\mathbb P$ is said to be with {\em universal coefficient semifield}, if $\mathbb P=\mathbb {Q}_{\rm {sf}}(X_{1;t_0},\ldots,X_{n;t_0})$ for some seed $t_0$ of $\mathcal S$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
differentia: $\mathbb P=\mathbb {Q}_{\rm {sf}}(X_{1;t_0},\ldots,X_{n;t_0})$ for some seed $t_0$ of $\mathcal S$

nodes.name: Coefficient matrices and extended exchange matrices
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal S$ be a seed pattern of geometric type with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$. We know that each $\mathscr X$-variable $X_{k;t}$ has the form $$X_{k;t}=Z_1^{c_{1k}^t}\cdots Z_m^{c_{mk}^t}.$$ The matrix $C_t:=(c_{ij}^t)_{m\times n}$ is called the {\em coefficient matrix} at $t$ and the $(n+m)\times n$ matrix $\widetilde B_t=\begin{pmatrix}B_t\\C_t\end{pmatrix}$ is called the {\em extended exchange matrix} at $t$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: For geometric type, the exponents of X_{k;t} in Z_1..Z_m form the coefficient matrix C_t; stacking B_t over C_t gives the extended exchange matrix.
nodes.label: def:extended_exchange_mat

nodes.name: Extended exchange matrices mutate by matrix mutation
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Proposition 5.8]{FZ}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal S$ be a seed pattern of geometric type. Then for any edge $t^{~\underline{\quad k \quad}}~ t^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb T_n$, we have $\widetilde B_{t^\prime}=\mu_k(\widetilde B_t)$, where $\widetilde B_t$ and $\widetilde B_{t^\prime}$ are the extended exchange matrices at $t$ and $t^\prime$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal S$ be a seed pattern  of geometric type.
conclusions: for any edge $t^{~\underline{\quad k \quad}}~ t^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb T_n$, we have $\widetilde B_{t^\prime}=\mu_k(\widetilde B_t)$

nodes.name: Cluster Poisson algebra
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal S_{\rm uc}$ be an $\mathscr X$-seed pattern with universal coefficient semifield. The {\em cluster Poisson algebra} $\mathcal X=\mathcal X(\mathcal S_{\rm uc})$ associated with $\mathcal S_{\rm uc}$ is the intersection $$\mathcal X=\bigcap\limits_{t\in\mathbb T_n} {\mathcal L}(t),$$ where ${\mathcal L}(t)=\mathbb {K}[X_{1;t}^{\pm1},\ldots,X_{n;t}^{\pm1}]$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
nodes.statement_short: The cluster Poisson algebra is the intersection over all seeds of the Laurent polynomial rings in the cluster Poisson variables.
nodes.label: defcpa

nodes.name: Cluster algebra and upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal S$ be an $\mathscr A$-seed pattern over a semifield $\mathbb P$. (i) The {\em cluster algebra} $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(\mathcal S)$ associated with $\mathcal S$ is the $\mathbb {KP}$-subalgebra of $\mathcal F$ generated by the cluster variables of $\mathcal S$, namely, $\mathcal A=\mathbb{KP}[A_{1;t},\ldots,A_{n;t}\mid t\in\mathbb T_n]$. (ii) The {\em upper cluster algebra} $\mathcal U=\mathcal U(\mathcal S)$ associated with $\mathcal S$ is the intersection $$\mathcal U=\bigcap\limits_{t\in\mathbb T_n} {\mathcal L}(t),$$ where ${\mathcal L}(t)=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t}^{\pm1}]$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
also_stated_at: The {\em upper cluster algebra} $\mathcal U$ is defined to be the algebra of global functions on the cluster $K_2$-variety, and the {\em cluster Poisson algebra} $\mathcal X$ is defined to be the algebra of the global functions on the cluster Poisson variety.
nodes.statement_short: The cluster algebra is generated by all cluster variables; the upper cluster algebra is the intersection of all Laurent polynomial rings L(t).

nodes.name: Laurent phenomenon and positivity
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and initial seed $t_0$. The following statements hold. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] {\rm (}\cite{FZ}{\rm ).} Each cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal A$ can be written as a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {ZP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$. \item[(ii)] {\rm (}\cite{GHKK}{\rm ).} The coefficients of the above Laurent polynomial are in $\mathbb{ NP}$. \item[(iii)] {\rm (}\cite{FZ1}{\rm ).} If $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$, then each cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal A$ can be written as a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and initial seed $t_0$.
$\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$
conclusions: Each  cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal A$ can be written as a  Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {ZP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$.
The coefficients of the above Laurent polynomial are in $\mathbb{ NP}$.

The coefficients of the above Laurent polynomial are in $\mathbb{ NP}$.

assumptions: $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$
conclusions:
each cluster  variable $A_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal A$ can be written as a  Laurent polynomial in
$\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$

also_stated_at: One remarkable feature of cluster algebras is the Laurent phenomenon \cite{FZ}, that is, for any given cluster $A_{t_0}=(A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0})$, each cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ can be written as $$A_{k;t}=\frac{P(A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0})}{A_{1;t_0}^{d_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{d_n}},$$ where $P$ is a polynomial in variables from $A_{t_0}$ such that $A_{i;t_0}$ does not divide $P$ for any $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Cluster variables are Laurent polynomials in any initial cluster, with positive coefficients; integer polynomial coefficients in geometric type.

nodes.name: Full rank upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement: A geometric upper cluster algebra with initial seed $t_0$ is called a {\em full rank upper cluster algebra} if its initial extended exchange matrix $\widetilde B_{t_0}$ has full rank.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
differentia: its initial extended exchange matrix $\widetilde B_{t_0}$ has full rank
also_stated_at: The upper cluster algebra is said to be {\em full rank} or {\em primitive} if $\widetilde{B}_t$ is.

nodes.name: Full rank is seed independent
nodes.statement: For a full rank upper cluster algebra $\mathcal U$, we know that every extended exchange matrix $\widetilde B_t$ of $\mathcal U$ has full rank, by Proposition \ref{prorank}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Starfish Theorem
nodes.statement: {\rm (}Starfish Theorem, \cite[Corollary 1.9]{BFZ}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$. Then we have $$\mathcal U=\bigcap\limits_{i=0}^n{\mathcal L}(t_i),$$ where $t_j=\mu_j(t_0)$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$ and ${\mathcal L}(t_i)=\mathbb{KP}[A_{1;t_i}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_i}^{\pm1}]$ for $i=0,1,\ldots,n$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$  be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$.
nodes.statement_short: A full rank upper cluster algebra is the intersection of the n+1 Laurent rings of a seed and its one-step mutations.
nodes.label: proup

nodes.name: Connectedness of seeds containing given cluster variables
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Theorem 10]{CL1}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$. Then the seeds of $\mathcal A$ whose clusters contain particular cluster variables form a connected subgraph of the exchange graph of $\mathcal A$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$.
conclusions: the seeds of  $\mathcal A$ whose clusters contain particular cluster variables form a connected subgraph of the exchange graph  of $\mathcal A$
nodes.label: thmacon

nodes.name: Seeds sharing n-1 cluster variables are adjacent
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Corollary 3]{CL1}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and $t_1,t_2$ two seeds of $\mathcal A$. If $t_1$ and $t_2$ have at least $n-1$ common cluster variables, then in the exchange graph of $\mathcal A$ either $t_1$ and $t_2$ represent the same vertex or there is an edge between $t_1$ and $t_2$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and $t_1,t_2$ two seeds of $\mathcal A$.
$t_1$ and $t_2$ have at least $n-1$ common cluster variables
conclusions: in the exchange graph of $\mathcal A$ either $t_1$ and $t_2$ represent the same vertex or there is an edge between $t_1$ and $t_2$
nodes.label: corn-1

nodes.name: Acyclic cluster algebra
nodes.statement:
Recall that a cluster algebra is {\em acyclic} if it has an acyclic seed: a seed with an exchange matrix $B=(b_{ij})$, such
that there is no sequence of indices $i_1,\ldots,i_{\ell+1}\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with  $i_{\ell+1}=i_1$ and $b_{i_j,i_{j+1}}>0$  for $j=1,\ldots,\ell$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras

nodes.name: Acyclic cluster algebras equal their upper cluster algebras
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite{BFZ}, \cite[Theorem 2]{M}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be an acyclic cluster algebra and $\mathcal U$ the corresponding upper cluster algebra. Then $\mathcal A=\mathcal U$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Basics on cluster algebras and cluster Poisson algebras
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be an acyclic cluster algebra and $\mathcal U$ the corresponding upper cluster algebra.
nodes.label: proacyclic

nodes.name: d-vector and numerator polynomial
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
also_stated_at: The vector $${\bf d}^{t_0}(A_{k;t})=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)^{\rm T}$$ is called the {\em $d$-vector} of $A_{k;t}$ with respect to $A_{t_0}$ and the polynomial $P$ is called the {\em numerator polynomial} of $A_{k;t}$ with respect to $A_{t_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Writing a Laurent polynomial M as P_M over a monomial with P_M not divisible by any A_j, the exponents form the d-vector and P_M the numerator polynomial.

nodes.name: Additivity of d-vectors
nodes.statement: Notice that for any $0\neq M,N\in\mathcal L(t_0)$, we have $${\bf d}^{t_0}(M\cdot N)={\bf d}^{t_0}(M)+{\bf d}^{t_0}(N).$$
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
nodes.statement_short: d-vectors are additive under products.
nodes.label: rmkdadd

nodes.name: F-polynomial
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable integer matrix and $\mathcal A$ a principal coefficient cluster algebra at $t_0$ with $B_{t_0}=B$. Let $A_{k;t}$ be a cluster variable of $\mathcal A$, which can be written as a Laurent polynomial in $$\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_n][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}],$$ by the Laurent phenomenon. The polynomial $$F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n):=A_{k;t}\mid _{A_{1;t_0}=\ldots=A_{n;t_0}=1}\in\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_n],$$ which only depends on $(B,t_0;k,t)$, is called an {\em $F$-polynomial} of $B$. {\em Sometimes we view $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$ as a polynomial in new variables $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ due to the convention in \cite{FZ3}. }
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
also_stated_at: Let $B$ be an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable integer matrix. The {\em $F$-polynomial} $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$ associated with $(B,t_0; k,t)$ may be constructed by an explicit recursion or using the cluster algebra $\mathcal A$ with principal coefficients \cite{FZ3} associated with $(B,t_0)$: Let $A_{t_0}=(A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0})$ be the initial cluster of $\mathcal A$ and $A_{k;t}$ a cluster variable of $\mathcal A$. In this case, the cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ can be written as a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_n][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$. Then the $F$-polynomial of $A_{k;t}$ is the specialization given by $$F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n):=A_{k;t}\mid _{A_{1;t_0}=\ldots=A_{n;t_0}=1}\in\mathbb Z[Z_1,\ldots,Z_n].$$
nodes.statement_short: F-polynomial of a cluster variable in a principal coefficient cluster algebra: specialise all initial cluster variables to 1.
nodes.label: deffp

nodes.name: F-polynomials are not divisible by any Y_j
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Proposition 5.2]{FZ3}{\rm ).} The $F$-polynomial $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$ is not divisible by any $Y_j$.
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
nodes.label: profy

nodes.name: D-matrices and F-matrices
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable matrix and $t_0$ a vertex of $\mathbb T_n$. (i) {\rm (}\cite[(7.6), (7.7)]{FZ3}{\rm ).} The matrix $D_t^{B;t_0}=(d_{ij;t}^{B;t_0})$ is uniquely determined by the initial condition $B_{t_0}=B$ and $D_{t_0}^{B;t_0}=-I_n$, together with the following recurrence relations: \begin{equation} d_{ij;t^\prime}^{B;t_0}=\begin{cases}d_{ij;t}^{B;t_0}, & \text{if } j\neq k;\\ -d_{ik;t}^{B;t_0}+{\rm max}\{\sum\limits_{b_{lk}^t>0}d_{il;t}^{B;t_0} b_{lk}^t, \sum\limits_{b_{lk}^t<0} -d_{il;t}^{B;t_0}b_{lk}^t\}, &\text{if } j=k,\end{cases}\nonumber \end{equation} for any edge $t^{~\underline{\quad k \quad}}~ t^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb T_n$. The matrices $\{D_t^{B;t_0}\}_{t\in\mathbb T_n}$ are called the {\em $D$-matrices} of $B$. (ii) {\rm (}\cite[Definition 2.6]{FG1}{\rm ).} Let $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be the $F$-polynomial given in Definition \ref{deffp}, and $f_{ik;t}^{B;t_0}$ be the maximal exponent of $Z_i$ appearing in $F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$. The vector $${\bf f}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}=(f_{1k;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,f_{nk;t}^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}$$ is called an {\em $f$-vector} of $B$ and the matrix $F_t^{B;t_0}=(f_{ij;t}^{B;t_0})_{n\times n}$ is called an {\em $F$-matrix} of $B$.
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
nodes.statement_short: D-matrices defined by a tropical recurrence from -I_n; f-vectors record maximal exponents of Z_i in F-polynomials, forming F-matrices.
nodes.label: defdf

nodes.name: Columns of D-matrices are d-vectors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with initial exchange matrix $B$ at $t_0$. Then the $k$-th column vector ${\bf d}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$ of $D_{t}^{B;t_0}$ is exactly the $d$-vector ${\bf d}^{t_0}(A_{k;t})$ of $A_{k;t}$ with respect to $A_{t_0}$, by \cite[(7.7)]{FZ3}.
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with initial exchange matrix $B$ at $t_0$.
conclusions: the $k$-th column vector ${\bf d}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}$ of $D_{t}^{B;t_0}$ is exactly the $d$-vector ${\bf d}^{t_0}(A_{k;t})$ of  $A_{k;t}$ with respect to $A_{t_0}$

nodes.name: d-vectors change only at the mutated index
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra and $M$ a non-zero element in $\mathcal U$. Let $t_0, t_1$ be two seeds of $\mathcal U$ with $t_1=\mu_k(t_0)$. Let ${\bf d}=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)^{\rm T}$ and ${\bf d}^\prime=(d_1^\prime,\ldots,d_n^\prime)^{\rm T}$ be the $d$-vectors of $M$ with respect to $t_0$ and $t_1$ respectively. Then $d_i=d_i^\prime$ for any $i\neq k$.
nodes.section: 2.2 \texorpdfstring{$d$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$f$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$g$}{Lg}-vectors, \texorpdfstring{$c$}{Lg}-vectors and \texorpdfstring{$F$}{Lg}-polynomials
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be an  upper cluster algebra and $M$ a non-zero element in $\mathcal U$.
Let $t_0, t_1$ be two seeds of $\mathcal U$ with $t_1=\mu_k(t_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: The d-vectors of an element with respect to adjacent seeds t_0, mu_k(t_0) agree off index k.
nodes.label: prodvectors

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.25
nodes.statement: The proof is the same as that of \cite[Proposition 2.5]{RS}.

nodes.statement_short: Same argument as Reading-Stella, Proposition 2.5.

nodes.name: Canonical expressions
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable matrix and $$\{F_{1;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,F_{n;t}^{B;t_0}\}_{t\in\mathbb T_n}$$ the $F$-polynomials given in Definition \ref{deffp}. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] {\rm (}\cite[Corollary 6.3]{FZ3}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with principal coefficients at $t_0$ and with $B_{t_0}=B$. Then for any cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal A$, there exists a unique vector ${\bf g}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}=(g_{1k;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,g_{nk;t}^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}\in \mathbb Z^n$ such that \begin{eqnarray} A_{k;t}=A_{t_0}^{{\bf g}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}}\cdot F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(\widehat X_{1;t_0},\ldots,\widehat X_{n;t_0}),\nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $A_{t_0}^{{\bf g}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}}=\prod\limits_{i=1}^nA_{i;t}^{g_{ik;t}^{B;t_0}}$, $\widehat X_{j;t_0}=X_{j;t_0}\prod\limits_{i=1}^nA_{i;t_0}^{b_{ij}^{t_0}}=Z_j\prod\limits_{i=1}^nA_{i;t_0}^{b_{ij}^{t_0}}$. \item[(ii)] {\rm (}\cite[Proposition 1.1]{NZ}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal X$ be the cluster Poisson algebra with $B_{t_0}=B$. Then for any cluster Poisson variable $X_{k;t}$ of $\mathcal X$, there exists a unique vector ${\bf c}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}=(c_{1k;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,c_{nk;t}^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}\in \mathbb Z^n$ such that $$X_{k;t}=X_{t_0}^{{\bf c}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}}\cdot \prod\limits_{i=1}^n(F_{i;t}^{B;t_0}(X_{1;t_0},\ldots,X_{n;t_0}))^{b_{ik}^t}.$$ \end{itemize}

nodes.statement_short: Cluster variables = A^g F(hat X) (principal coefficients); cluster Poisson variables = X^c prod F_i^{b_ik} (separation formulas).
nodes.label: thmsf

nodes.name: Separation formula for cluster variables
nodes.statement: A_{k;t}=A_{t_0}^{{\bf g}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}}\cdot F_{k;t}^{B;t_0}(\widehat X_{1;t_0},\ldots,\widehat X_{n;t_0}),\nonumber

nodes.label: eqnsf

nodes.name: g-vectors and c-vectors
nodes.statement: Keep the notations of Theorem \ref{thmsf}. (i) The vector ${\bf g}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}=(g_{1k;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,g_{nk;t}^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}\in \mathbb Z^n,$ which only depends on $(B,t_0;k,t)$, is called a {\em $g$-vector} of $B$. The matrix $G_t^{B;t_0}=({\bf g}_{ij;t}^{B;t_0})_{n\times n}$ is called a {\em $G$-matrix} of $B$ at $t$. (ii) The vector ${\bf c}_{k;t}^{B;t_0}=(c_{1k;t}^{B;t_0},\ldots,c_{nk;t}^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}\in \mathbb Z^n,$ which only depends on $(B,t_0;k,t)$, is called a {\em $c$-vector} of $B$. The matrix $C_t^{B;t_0}=({\bf c}_{ij;t}^{B;t_0})_{n\times n}$ is called a {\em $C$-matrix} of $B$ at $t$.

nodes.name: Tropical duality of C- and G-matrices
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[(3.11)]{NZ}, \cite[Corollary 4.11]{CL}{\rm ).} Let $B$ be an $n\times n$ skew-symmetrizable matrix and $S$ a skew-symmetrizer of $B$. Then for any vertices $t_0, t\in\mathbb T_n$, we have $$SC_t^{B;t_0}S^{-1}(G_t^{B;t_0})^{\rm T}=I_n.$$

nodes.name: Compatibility degrees
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra and $\mathbb A$ the set of cluster variables of $\mathcal A$. (i) {\rm (}\cite[Definition 8]{CL1}{\rm ).} The $d$-compatibility degree $(-\mid\mid -)_d: \mathbb A\times \mathbb A\rightarrow\mathbb Z_{\geq-1}$ is defined by $$(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d:=d_{ij;t}^{B_{t_0};t_0},$$ where $d_{ij;t}^{B_{t_0};t_0}$ is the $(i,j)$-entry of the $D$-matrix $D_t^{B_{t_0};t_0}$. (ii) {\rm (}\cite[Definition 4.9]{FG}{\rm ).} The $f$-compatibility degree $(-\mid\mid -)_f: \mathbb A\times \mathbb A\rightarrow\mathbb N$ is defined by $$(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_f:=f_{ij;t}^{B_{t_0};t_0},$$ where $f_{ij;t}^{B_{t_0};t_0}$ is the $(i,j)$-entry of the $F$-matrix $F_t^{B_{t_0};t_0}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Compatibility degrees on the set of cluster variables
nodes.statement_short: d- and f-compatibility degrees of a pair of cluster variables are entries of the D-matrix and F-matrix respectively.

nodes.name: Properties of d- and f-compatibility degrees
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Theorem 11, Remark 2]{CL1}, \cite[Theorems 3.3, 4.18]{FG}{\rm ).} The $d$-compatibility degree $(-\mid\mid -)_d$ and the $f$-compatibility degree $(-\mid\mid -)_f$ have the following properties. \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] They are well-defined. \item[(2)] The following statements are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] There exists a cluster $A_{t^\prime}$ containing both $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$; \item[(ii)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d\leq 0$; \item[(iii)] $(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_d\leq 0$; \item[(iv)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_f= 0$; \item[(v)] $(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_f=0$. \end{itemize} \item[(3)] The following statements are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] There exists no cluster $A_{t^\prime}$ containing both $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$; \item[(ii)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d>0$; \item[(iii)] $(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_d>0$; \item[(iv)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_f>0$; \item[(v)]$(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_f>0$. \end{itemize} \item[(4)] The following statements are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $A_{j;t}=A_{i;t_0}$; \item[(ii)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d<0$; \item[(iii)]$(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_d<0$; \item[(iv)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d=-1$; \item[(v)] $(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_d=-1$. \end{itemize} \item[(5)] The following statements are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $A_{i;t_0}\neq A_{j;t}$ and there exists a cluster $A_{t^\prime}$ containing both $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$; \item[(ii)] $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d=0$; \item[(iii)] $(A_{j;t}\mid\mid A_{i;t_0})_d=0$; \end{itemize} \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.3 Compatibility degrees on the set of cluster variables
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility degrees are well defined and detect compatibility (<=0, =0), incompatibility (>0) and equality (=-1) of cluster variables.
nodes.label: rmkdf

nodes.name: d-compatibility degree on the upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement: (i) Roughly speaking, the integer $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d$ is defined to be the $i$-th component of the $d$-vector of $A_{j;t}$ with respect to $A_{t_0}$. By Proposition \ref{prodvectors} and Theorem \ref{thmacon}, the $d$-compatibility degree $(-\mid\mid -)_d$ is actually a well-defined function on $\mathbb A\times (\mathcal U\backslash\{0\})$, where $\mathcal U$ is the corresponding upper cluster algebra. (ii) By Remark \ref{rmkdadd}, for any $0\neq M,N\in\mathcal U$, we have $$(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid M\cdot N)_d=(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d+(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid N)_d.$$

nodes.statement_short: The d-compatibility degree extends to a well-defined additive function on cluster variables times nonzero elements of U.

nodes.name: d-compatibility with cluster monomials
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and $A_{k;t_0}$ a cluster variable of $\mathcal A$. Let $t$ be a seed of $\mathcal A$ and $M=A_{1;t}^{c_1}\cdots A_{n;t}^{c_n}$ a cluster monomial in $t$. Denote $I=\{i\mid c_i>0\}$. The following statements hold. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)]If $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d<0$, then there exists $j_0\in I$ such that $A_{k;t_0}=A_{j_0;t}$. Namely, $A_{k;t_0}$ appears in $M$. \item[(ii)] If $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d\leq0$, then $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i;t})_d\leq0$ for any $i\in I$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.32
nodes.statement: (i) By $c_1,\ldots,c_n\geq0$ and $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d<0$, we have $$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d=\sum_{i=1}^nc_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i;t})_d=\sum_{i\in I}c_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i;t})_d<0.$$ So there must exist some $j_0\in I$ such that $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j_0;t})_d<0$. Then by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4), we get $A_{k;t_0}=A_{j_0;t}$. (ii) Assume by contradiction there exists some $i_0\in I$ such that $$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i_0;t})_d>0.$$ Then by $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_d=\sum\limits_{i\in I}c_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i;t})_d\leq0$, there must exist some $i_1\in I$ such that $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i_1;t})_d<0$. So we get $A_{k;t_0}=A_{i_1;t}$, by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4). Thus $A_{i_0;t}$ and $A_{k;t_0}=A_{i_1;t}$ are in the same cluster. Then by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (2), we get $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i_0;t})_d\leq 0$. This contradicts $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i_0;t})_d>0$. So $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid A_{i;t})_d\leq0$ for any $i\in I$.

(i) By $c_1,\ldots,c_n\geq0$ and $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_d<0$, we have
$$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_d=\sum_{i=1}^nc_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i;t})_d=\sum_{i\in I}c_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i;t})_d<0.$$
So there must exist some $j_0\in I$ such that $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{j_0;t})_d<0$. Then by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4), we get $A_{k;t_0}=A_{j_0;t}$.

nodes.name: Part (ii)

(ii) Assume by contradiction there exists some $i_0\in I$ such that
$$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i_0;t})_d>0.$$ Then by $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_d=\sum\limits_{i\in I}c_i(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i;t})_d\leq0$, there must exist some $i_1\in I$ such that $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i_1;t})_d<0$. So we get $A_{k;t_0}=A_{i_1;t}$, by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4). Thus $A_{i_0;t}$ and $A_{k;t_0}=A_{i_1;t}$ are in the same cluster. Then by  Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (2), we get $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i_0;t})_d\leq 0$. This contradicts  $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i_0;t})_d>0$. So $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{i;t})_d\leq0$ for any $i\in I$.

nodes.name: Compatible cluster variables
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra and $\mathbb A$  the set of cluster variables of $\mathcal A$.
We say that two cluster variables $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ of $\mathcal A$ are {\em compatible}  if there exists a cluster $A_{t^\prime}$ of $\mathcal A$ containing both $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$, which is equivalent to $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{j;t})_d\leq 0$, by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (2).
nodes.section: 2.3 Compatibility degrees on the set of cluster variables

nodes.name: Compatible set
nodes.statement: A subset $U$ of $\mathbb A$  is called a  {\em compatible set} if any two cluster variables in $U$ are compatible.
nodes.section: 2.3 Compatibility degrees on the set of cluster variables

nodes.name: Clusters are maximal compatible sets
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Theorem 13]{CL1}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be a cluster algebra and $\mathbb A$ the set of cluster variables of $\mathcal A$. Then \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] a subset $U$ of $\mathbb A$ is a compatible set if and only if it is a subset of some cluster of $\mathcal A$; \item[(ii)] a subset $U$ of $\mathbb A$ is a maximal compatible set if and only it is a cluster of $\mathcal A$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Integral domain
nodes.statement:
Recall that an integral domain is a non-zero commutative
ring in which the product of any two nonzero elements is nonzero.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains

nodes.name: Units of R
nodes.statement: From now on, we always assume that $R$ is an integral domain and we denote by $R^\times$  the set of invertible elements in $R$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains

nodes.name: Associate elements
nodes.statement:
Two non-zero elements $r_1,r_2\in R$
are {\em associate} if there exists some invertible element $s\in R^\times$ such that $r_2=sr_1$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains

nodes.name: Irreducible element
nodes.statement:
A non-zero, non-invertible element $r$ in  $R$ is {\em irreducible}, if
any factorization $r=r_1r_2$ with $r_1,r_2\in R$ implies that either $r_1$ or $r_2$ belongs to $R^\times$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains
differentia: any factorization $r=r_1r_2$ with $r_1,r_2\in R$ implies that either $r_1$ or $r_2$ belongs to $R^\times$

nodes.name: Prime element
nodes.statement:
A non-zero, non-invertible element $r$ in $R$ is {\em prime},  if
whenever $r\mid r_1r_2$ for some  $r_1,r_2\in R$, then $r\mid r_1$ or $r\mid r_2$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains
differentia: whenever $r\mid r_1r_2$ for some  $r_1,r_2\in R$, then $r\mid r_1$ or $r\mid r_2$

nodes.name: Prime elements are irreducible
nodes.statement:
Every prime element is
irreducible, but the converse is not true in general.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains

nodes.name: Factorial domain
nodes.statement: An integral domain $R$ is {\em factorial} if the following hold: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Every non-zero, non-invertible element $r\in R$ can be written as a product $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ of irreducible elements $a_i\in R$. \item[(ii)] If $a_1\cdots a_s=b_1\cdots b_t$ with $a_i,b_j\in R$ irreducible for all $i$ and $j$, then $s=t$ and there is a bijection $\sigma:\{1,\ldots,s\}\rightarrow \{1,\ldots,s\}$ such that $a_i$ and $b_{\sigma(i)}$ are associate for all $1\leq i\leq s$. \end{itemize} Factorial domains are also known as {\em unique factorization domains}.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains
differentia:
Every non-zero, non-invertible element $r\in R$ can be written as a product
$r=a_1\cdots a_s$ of irreducible elements $a_i\in R$.

nodes.name: Irreducibles are prime in factorial domains
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that in a factorial domain, all irreducible elements are prime.
nodes.section: 2.4 Unique factorization domains
assumptions: in a factorial domain

nodes.name: Units and irreducibility of cluster variables
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a geometric cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and $\mathcal U$ the corresponding upper cluster algebra. Then the following statements hold. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $\mathcal A^\times=\{\lambda Z_1^{c_1}\cdots Z_m^{c_m}\mid \lambda\in\mathbb K^\times,\; c_1,\ldots,c_m\in \mathbb Z\}$. \item[(b)] Any cluster variable is irreducible in $\mathcal A$. \end{itemize} \item[(ii)] \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $\mathcal U^\times=\{\lambda Z_1^{c_1}\cdots Z_m^{c_m}\mid \lambda\in\mathbb K^\times,\; c_1,\ldots,c_m\in \mathbb Z\}$. \item[(b)] Any cluster variable is irreducible in $\mathcal U$. \end{itemize} \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Valuation pairing
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra and $\mathbb A$ the set of cluster variables of $\mathcal U$. The pairing \begin{eqnarray} (-\mid\mid -)_v:\mathbb A\times\mathcal U&\rightarrow&\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\nonumber\\ (A_{k;t},M)&\mapsto&{\rm max}\{s\in\mathbb N\mid M/A_{k;t}^s\in\mathcal U\}\nonumber \end{eqnarray} is called the {\em valuation pairing} on $\mathcal U$.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
also_stated_at: To each pair $(A_{k;t},M)$ consisting of a cluster variable $A_{k;t}$ and an element $M$ in $\mathcal U$, it associates the largest integer $s$ (possibly infinity) such that $M/A_{k;t}^s$ still belongs to $\mathcal U$. We write $(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M)_v=s$.
nodes.statement_short: (A_{k;t} || M)_v is the largest s with M / A_{k;t}^s still in U (possibly infinity).

nodes.name: Zero valuation criterion
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $(A_{k;t}\mid\mid  M)_v=0$ if and only if $M/A_{k;t}\notin \mathcal U$.

conclusions: $(A_{k;t}\mid\mid  M)_v=0$ if and only if $M/A_{k;t}\notin \mathcal U$

nodes.name: Valuation pairing on cluster variables of a seed
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra with a seed $t$ and $M$ a cluster variable in $t$. Then $$(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M)_v=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if}\;M=A_{k;t};\\0,&\text{if}\;M=A_{j;t}\;\text{and}\;j\neq k.\end{cases}$$

nodes.statement_short: (A_{k;t}||M)_v is 1 if M=A_{k;t} and 0 if M is another variable of the same seed.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction for (i); for (ii) expand M in A_{n;t_0}, rewrite in the adjacent seed and use factoriality of the Laurent ring to bound the power.

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: (i) Assume by contradiction that $M/A_{k;t_0}^{m+1}\in \mathcal U$, then $$M/A_{k;t_0}^m=A_{k;t_0}\cdot (M/A_{k;t_0}^{m+1})\in\mathcal U.$$ This is a contradiction. So $M/A_{k;t_0}^{m+1}\notin \mathcal U$.
nodes.statement_short: If M/A^{m+1} were in U, multiplying by A gives M/A^m in U.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement:
(ii) Without loss of generality, we can assume that $k=n$.
As an element in $${\mathcal L}(t_0)=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}]=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_0}^{\pm 1}][A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}],$$
 $M$ can be written as
$$M=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_0}^sL_s,$$
where $L_s$ is a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_0}^{\pm 1}]$, i.e., $L_s$ does not contain any $A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}$.
By $M\neq 0$, we know that there exists some $s_0$ such that $L_{s_0}\neq 0$.  Let $t_1=\mu_{n}(t_0)$ and thus $t_0=\mu_n(t_1)$. Applying the exchange relation, we have
 $$A_{i;t_0}=A_{i;t_1}\;\;\text{and}\;\;\; A_{n;t_0}=A_{n;t_1}^{-1}P$$
where $i=1,\ldots,n-1$ and $P\in\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$ is the $n$-th exchange  binomial of the seed $t_1$. Now each $L_s$ can be also viewed as a Laurent polynomial in  $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$. By our assumption in Subsection \ref{rmkexbi}, we know that $P$ is not invertible in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$.
Then by the fact that $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$ is factorial and $L_{s_0}$ belongs to  $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$, we know that there must exist some $m_0$ large enough such that $$L_{s_0}/P^{m_0}\notin \mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}].$$ Set $m=m_0+s_0$. Then we know that
$$
M/A_{n;t_0}^m=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_0}^{s-m}L_s=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_1}^{m-s}(L_s/P^{m-s})\nonumber
$$
cannot be a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_1}^{\pm1}]$. So $M/A_{n;t_0}^m$ is not in $\mathcal U$. Then by (i), we know that  $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v<m<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the divisibility of M by A_{k;t_0} via the adjacent seed.

nodes.name: WLOG k=n
nodes.statement:
Without loss of generality, we can assume that $k=n$.
As an element in $${\mathcal L}(t_0)=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}]=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_0}^{\pm 1}][A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}],$$
 $M$ can be written as
$$M=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_0}^sL_s,$$
where $L_s$ is a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_0}^{\pm 1}]$, i.e., $L_s$ does not contain any $A_{n;t_0}^{\pm 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to k=n and expand M in powers of A_{n;t_0}.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Pass to adjacent seed
nodes.statement:
By $M\neq 0$, we know that there exists some $s_0$ such that $L_{s_0}\neq 0$.  Let $t_1=\mu_{n}(t_0)$ and thus $t_0=\mu_n(t_1)$. Applying the exchange relation, we have
 $$A_{i;t_0}=A_{i;t_1}\;\;\text{and}\;\;\; A_{n;t_0}=A_{n;t_1}^{-1}P$$
where $i=1,\ldots,n-1$ and $P\in\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$ is the $n$-th exchange  binomial of the seed $t_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a nonzero coefficient L_{s_0}; rewrite via the exchange relation in t_1.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Use non-invertibility of P
nodes.statement:
Now each $L_s$ can be also viewed as a Laurent polynomial in  $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$. By our assumption in Subsection \ref{rmkexbi}, we know that $P$ is not invertible in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$.
Then by the fact that $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$ is factorial and $L_{s_0}$ belongs to  $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}]$, we know that there must exist some $m_0$ large enough such that $$L_{s_0}/P^{m_0}\notin \mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm 1},\ldots, A_{n-1;t_1}^{\pm 1}].$$
nodes.statement_short: By the standing assumption P is not invertible, so a high power of P does not divide L_{s_0}.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Conclude finiteness
nodes.statement:
Set $m=m_0+s_0$. Then we know that
$$
M/A_{n;t_0}^m=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_0}^{s-m}L_s=\sum\limits_{s\in\mathbb Z}A_{n;t_1}^{m-s}(L_s/P^{m-s})\nonumber
$$
cannot be a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_1}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_1}^{\pm1}]$. So $M/A_{n;t_0}^m$ is not in $\mathcal U$. Then by (i), we know that  $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v<m<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: M/A^m is not a Laurent polynomial in t_1, hence not in U; (i) gives finiteness.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: (iii) This follows from (ii) and the fact $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  0)_v=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: From (ii) and value at 0.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Parts (iv),(v)
nodes.statement: The results in (iv) and (v) follow from the definition of the valuation pairing.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Local factorization
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra and $t$ a seed of $\mathcal U$. Let $M=N\cdot L$ be a factorization in $\mathcal U$. If $N$ is a cluster monomial in $t$ and $L\in\mathcal U$ satisfies $(A_{k;t}\mid\mid L)_v=0$, that is, $L/A_{k;t}\notin \mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$, we call $M=N\cdot L$ a {\em local factorization} of $M$ with respect to $t$.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: M = N L with N a cluster monomial in t and L divisible by no cluster variable of t.
nodes.label: deflocal

nodes.name: Existence of local factorization
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$. Then any $0\neq M\in\mathcal U$ admits a local factorization with respect to $t_0$.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be an upper cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P$ and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$.
conclusions: any $0\neq M\in\mathcal U$ admits a local factorization with respect to $t_0$
nodes.label: proexist

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.5
nodes.statement: We first define a cluster monomial $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ in $t_0$. Let $m_1:=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid M)_v$ and $m_2,\ldots,m_n$ are defined by induction. If $m_{k}$ has been defined, $m_{k+1}$ is defined as follows: $$m_{k+1}:=(A_{k+1;t_0}\mid\mid \frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k;t_0}^{m_k}})_v.$$ Thus the non-negative integers $m_1,\ldots,m_n$ are defined. So we get a cluster monomial $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ in $t_0$ and we know that $L:=M/N\in\mathcal U$. Now we show that $L=M/N$ satisfies $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v=0$, that is, $L/A_{k;t_0}\notin\mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. Assume by contradiction that there exists some $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $$L/A_{k;t_0}=\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}}\in\mathcal U.$$ Thus we get $$\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}}=A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}(L/A_{k;t_0})\in\mathcal U,$$ which contradicts the choice of $m_k$. So $L/A_{k;t_0}\notin\mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. Thus $M=N\cdot L$ is a local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: Construct N by successively extracting maximal powers of each initial cluster variable; maximality gives the local factorization.

nodes.name: Construct N
nodes.statement:
We first define a cluster monomial $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ in $t_0$.  Let $m_1:=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v$ and  $m_2,\ldots,m_n$ are defined by induction. If $m_{k}$ has been defined, $m_{k+1}$ is defined as follows:
$$m_{k+1}:=(A_{k+1;t_0}\mid\mid  \frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k;t_0}^{m_k}})_v.$$
Thus the non-negative integers $m_1,\ldots,m_n$ are defined. So we get a cluster monomial $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ in $t_0$ and we know that $L:=M/N\in\mathcal U$.
nodes.statement_short: Define exponents m_k inductively via the valuation pairing.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Claim: L is not divisible
nodes.statement:
Now we show that $L=M/N$ satisfies $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v=0$, that is, $L/A_{k;t_0}\notin\mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. Assume by contradiction that there exists some $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that
$$L/A_{k;t_0}=\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}}\in\mathcal U.$$
Thus we get $$\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}}=A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}(L/A_{k;t_0})\in\mathcal U,$$
which contradicts the choice of $m_k$. So $L/A_{k;t_0}\notin\mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$.
nodes.statement_short: Show L/A_{k;t_0} not in U for all k.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Assume divisibility
nodes.statement:
Assume by contradiction that there exists some $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that
$$L/A_{k;t_0}=\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}}\in\mathcal U.$$
nodes.statement_short: Suppose L/A_{k;t_0} lies in U.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Contradict maximality
nodes.statement:
Thus we get $$\frac{M}{A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{k-1;t_0}^{m_{k-1}}A_{k;t_0}^{m_k+1}}=A_{k+1;t_0}^{m_{k+1}}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}(L/A_{k;t_0})\in\mathcal U,$$
which contradicts the choice of $m_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Then a larger power divides, contradicting the choice of m_k.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Claim holds
nodes.statement: So $L/A_{k;t_0}\notin\mathcal U$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$.
nodes.statement_short: L is not divisible by any initial cluster variable.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Thus $M=N\cdot L$ is a local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$.
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: M = N L is a local factorization.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Reduction Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$. Let $L$ be a non-zero element in $\mathcal U$ and $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ a cluster monomial in $t_0$. Then the following statements hold. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal U$ if and only if $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_k)$, where $s\in\mathbb N$, $t_k=\mu_k(t_0)$ and $$\mathcal L(t_k)=\mathbb{KP}[A_{1;t_k}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}^{\pm1}].$$ \item[(ii)] $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v={\rm max}\{s\in\mathbb N\mid L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_k)\}$. \item[(iii)] $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid N\cdot L)_v=m_k+(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$.
Let $L$ be a non-zero element in $\mathcal U$ and $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ a cluster monomial in $t_0$.
conclusions: $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal U$ if and only if $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_k)$
nodes.statement_short: For full rank U, divisibility by A_{k;t_0} is tested in the single Laurent ring L(mu_k t_0), and the valuation is additive on cluster monomials of t_0.
nodes.label: lemadd

nodes.name: Proof of the Reduction Lemma
nodes.statement: (i) By the Starfish Theorem \ref{proup}, we know that $\mathcal U=\bigcap\limits_{i=0}^n\mathcal L(t_i)$. Since $A_{k;t_0}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_i)$ for any $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\backslash\{k\}$, we have $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_i)$ for any $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\backslash\{k\}$. Thus we get that $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal U$ if and only if $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_k)$. (ii) This follows from (i) and the definition of the valuation pairing. (iii) Without loss of generality, we assume $k=1$. Since $A_{2;t_0}^{m_2}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_1)$ and by (ii), we have $$(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid N\cdot L)_v=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid \frac{N\cdot L}{A_{2;t_0}^{m_2}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}})_v=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdot L)_v.$$ Then by Proposition \ref{proind} (v), we get $$(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdot L)_v=m_1+(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v.$$ This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: Starfish Theorem: A_{k;t_0} is invertible in every L(t_i) except L(t_k).

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement:
(i)
By the Starfish Theorem \ref{proup}, we know that  $\mathcal U=\bigcap\limits_{i=0}^n\mathcal L(t_i)$. Since $A_{k;t_0}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_i)$ for any $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\backslash\{k\}$, we have $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_i)$ for any $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\backslash\{k\}$. Thus we get that $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal U$ if and only if $L/A_{k;t_0}^s\in\mathcal L(t_k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Starfish Theorem; only L(t_k) matters.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement: (ii) This follows from (i) and the definition of the valuation pairing.
nodes.statement_short: From (i) and the definition.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement:
(iii) Without loss of generality, we assume $k=1$. Since $A_{2;t_0}^{m_2}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_1)$ and by (ii), we have  $$(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid  N\cdot L)_v=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid  \frac{N\cdot L}{A_{2;t_0}^{m_2}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}})_v=(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid  A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdot L)_v.$$ Then by Proposition \ref{proind} (v), we get $$(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid   A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdot L)_v=m_1+(A_{1;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v.$$
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Remove invertible factors in L(t_1), then use Proposition 3.3 (v).
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Local unique factorization property
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$. Then any $0\neq M\in\mathcal U$ admits a unique local factorization with respect to $t_0$.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank upper cluster algebra and $t_0$ a seed of $\mathcal U$.
conclusions: any $0\neq M\in\mathcal U$ admits a unique local factorization with respect to $t_0$
also_stated_at: Using the valuation pairing we prove that any full rank upper cluster algebra has the following {\em local unique factorization property}: For each seed $t$ of $\mathcal U$, any non-zero element $M$ can be uniquely factorized as $M=N\cdot L$, where $N$ is a cluster monomial in $t$ and $L$ is an element in $\mathcal U$ not divisible by any cluster variable in $t$.
nodes.label: thmunique

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.7
nodes.statement: The existence of local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$ is known from Proposition \ref{proexist}. Now we show the uniqueness. Let $M=N\cdot L$ be a local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$, where $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ is a cluster monomial in $t_0$ and $L\in\mathcal U$ satisfies $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v=0$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. By the Reduction Lemma \ref{lemadd} (iii), we have $$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_v=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid N\cdot L)_v=m_k+(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid L)_v=m_k.$$ So $m_k=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid M)_v$ is uniquely determined by $M$. Namely, $N$ is uniquely determined by $M$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: Existence from Proposition 3.5; uniqueness since the Reduction Lemma forces m_k = (A_{k;t_0}||M)_v.

nodes.name: Existence
nodes.statement: The existence of local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$ is known  from Proposition \ref{proexist}.
nodes.statement_short: Existence by Proposition 3.5.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement:
Now we show the uniqueness.
Let $M=N\cdot L$ be a  local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$, where $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ is a cluster monomial in $t_0$ and $L\in\mathcal U$ satisfies $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v=0$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. By the Reduction Lemma \ref{lemadd} (iii), we have $$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  N\cdot L)_v=m_k+(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v=m_k.$$
So $m_k=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v$ is uniquely determined by $M$. Namely, $N$ is uniquely determined by $M$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Exponents of N are determined by the valuation pairing.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Apply Reduction Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $M=N\cdot L$ be a  local factorization of $M$ with respect to $t_0$, where $N=A_{1;t_0}^{m_1}\cdots A_{n;t_0}^{m_n}$ is a cluster monomial in $t_0$ and $L\in\mathcal U$ satisfies $(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v=0$ for $k=1,\ldots,n$. By the Reduction Lemma \ref{lemadd} (iii), we have $$(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  N\cdot L)_v=m_k+(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  L)_v=m_k.$$
nodes.statement_short: Reduction Lemma (iii) gives (A_{k;t_0}||M)_v = m_k.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: N determined
nodes.statement: So $m_k=(A_{k;t_0}\mid\mid  M)_v$ is uniquely determined by $M$. Namely, $N$ is uniquely determined by $M$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Hence N, and so L, is determined by M.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra

nodes.name: Non-unique local factorization without full rank
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be a geometric upper cluster algebra with initial extended exchange matrix $\widetilde B_{t_0}$ given by $$\widetilde B_{t_0}= B_{t_0}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Clearly, $\widetilde B_{t_0}$ is not full rank. Denote $t_1=\mu_1(t_0)$ and $t_3=\mu_3(t_0)$. Applying the exchange relations, we have the following equality. \begin{eqnarray} A_{1;t_0}A_{1;t_1}=A_{2;t_0}+1=A_{3;t_0}A_{3;t_3}. \end{eqnarray} It is easy to check that both $A_{1;t_1}$ and $A_{3;t_3}$ are not divisible by any cluster variable in $t_0$ (alternatively, one can also refer to Theorem \ref{thmup} (ii)). So the equality (\ref{eqnexample}) gives two different local factorizations of $A_{2;t_0}+1$ with respect to the initial seed $t_0$.
nodes.section: 3 The valuation pairing on an upper cluster algebra
nodes.statement_short: For a non-full-rank A_3-type matrix, A_{2;t_0}+1 has two different local factorizations.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.8
nodes.statement: (i)$\Longrightarrow$ (ii): By our assumption in Subsection \ref{rmkexbi}, we know that $A_{k;t}$ is not invertible in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. Now assume by contradiction that $A_{k;t}$ is not prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. Then there exists $M^\prime,L^\prime\in \mathcal L(t_k)$ such that both $M^\prime$ and $L^\prime$ are not divisible by $A_{k;t}$ in $\mathcal L(t_k)$, but the product $M^\prime\cdot L^\prime$ is divisible by $A_{k;t}$ in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. Since $M^\prime$ and $L^\prime$ are in $$\mathcal L(t_k)=\mathbb {K}[Z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,Z_m^{\pm1}][A_{1;t_k}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}^{\pm1}],$$ there exists a cluster monomial $A_{t_k}^{\bf v}$ in $t_k$ such that $M:=A_{t_k}^{\bf v}M^\prime$ and $L:=A_{t_k}^{\bf v} L^\prime$ belong to $\mathcal U$. Because $A_{t_k}^{\bf v}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_k)$, we know that both $M$ and $L$ are not divisible by $A_{k;t}$ in $\mathcal L(t_k)$, but the product $M\cdot L$ is divisible by $A_{k;t}$ in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. By the Reduction Lemma \ref{lemadd} (ii), we have $$(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M)_v=0=(A_{k;t}\mid\mid L)_v\;\; \text{but}\;\;(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M\cdot L)_v>0.$$ This contradicts that $(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M\cdot L)_v=(A_{k;t}\mid\mid M)_v+(A_{k;t}\mid\mid L)_v$ holds for any non-zero elements $M$ and $L$ in $\mathcal U$. Hence, $A_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. (ii)$\Longrightarrow$ (i): This follows from the Reduction Lemma \ref{lemadd} (ii). (ii)$\Longleftrightarrow$ (iii): Applying the exchange relation, we have $A_{k;t}A_{k;t_k}=P_{k;t}$. Since $A_{k;t_k}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_k)$, we know that $A_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$ if and only if $P_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$. (iii)$\Longleftrightarrow$ (iv): Notice that $\mathcal L(t_k)$ is a localization of $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}]$ at $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m, A_{1;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}$. Since $P_{k;t}=P_{k;t_k}$ is a binomial in $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}]$$ and it is not divisible by any $Z_i$ and $A_{j;t_k}$, we know that $P_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$ if and only if it is prime in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}]$. Because $P_{k;t}$ is actually a binomial in variables from $$\{Z_1,\ldots,Z_m, A_{1;t_k},\ldots,\widehat A_{k;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}\}=\{Z_1,\ldots,Z_m, A_{1;t},\ldots,\widehat A_{k;t},\ldots,A_{n;t}\},$$ we know that $P_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_k},\ldots,A_{n;t_k}]$ if and only if it is prime in $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t},\ldots,\widehat A_{k;t},\ldots,A_{n;t}].$$ Hence, $P_{k;t}$ is prime in $\mathcal L(t_k)$ if and only if it is prime in $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t},\ldots,\widehat A_{k;t},\ldots,A_{n;t}].$$ (iv)$\Longleftrightarrow$ (v): This follows from the fact that the polynomial ring $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t},\ldots,\widehat A_{k;t},\ldots,A_{n;t}]$$ is factorial.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.9
nodes.statement: (i)$\Longrightarrow$ (ii): By Theorem \ref{thmgls} (ii), we know that any cluster variable is irreducible in $\mathcal U$. Because $\mathcal U$ is factorial, we get that any irreducible element is prime in $\mathcal U$. In particular, any initial cluster variable $A_{k;t_0}$ is prime in $\mathcal U$. (ii)$\Longrightarrow$ (i): Let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by initial cluster variables. By the Laurent phenomenon, we have $$S^{-1}\mathcal U=\mathcal L(t_0)=\mathbb K[Z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,Z_m^{\pm1}][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}],$$ which is factorial. Since the initial cluster variables are prime in $\mathcal U$ and by Lemma \ref{lempp2} and Proposition \ref{pro:atomic}, we get that $\mathcal U$ is factorial. nodes.name: Part (i)

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement:
(ii)  We first show that  $P_M$ is not invertible in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}]$.
Since $M$ is a non-initial cluster variable and by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4), we have ${\bf d}\in\mathbb N^n$ and thus $A_{t_0}^{\bf d}\in\mathcal U$. By $M=P_M/A_{t_0}^{\bf d}$, we get $MA_{t_0}^{\bf d}=P_M$. By Theorem \ref{thmgls} (2), we know that both $M$ and $A_{t_0}^{\bf d}$ are not invertible in $\mathcal U$. So $P_M=MA_{t_0}^{\bf d}$ is not invertible in $\mathcal U$. Namely, we have
$$P_M\notin\mathcal U^\times=\{\lambda Z_1^{c_1}\cdots Z_m^{c_m}\mid \lambda\in\mathbb K^\times,\; c_1,\ldots,c_m\in \mathbb Z\}.$$
In particular, $P_M\notin\mathbb K^\times$. So $P_M$ is not invertible in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}]$.

We claim that $P_M$ is not divisible by any $Z_i$ and $A_{j;t_0}$ in $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}].$$ Since $P_M$ is a numerator polynomial, it is not divisible by any $A_{j;t_0}$. There are two approaches to prove $Z_i\nmid P_M$. The first one is that we prove the result by induction on the minimal length of a sequence of  mutations from the initial seed to the final seed. The second one is that we just view $Z_i$ as an exchangeable cluster variable. Then by the fact that $M$ and $Z_i$ are in the same cluster and  they are not equal, we get $(Z_i\mid\mid M)_d=0$, by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (5). This implies that $P_M$ is not divisible by $Z_i$.

We claim that  $P_M$ is not invertible in
$$\mathcal L(t_0)=\mathbb K[Z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,Z_m^{\pm1}][A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}].$$ This follows from the two facts that $P_M$ is not invertible in $$\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}]$$ and $P_M$ is not divisible by any $Z_i$ and $A_{j;t_0}$ in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}]$.




Now we show that $P_M$ is irreducible in $\mathcal L(t_0)$. Assume that $P_M=L_1L_2$ for some $L_1,L_2\in\mathcal L(t_0)$. We know that there exist vectors ${\bf v}_1,{\bf v}_2\in\mathbb N^n$ such that
$$U_1:=A_{t_0}^{{\bf v}_1}L_1\in\mathcal U\;\;\text{and}\;\;\; U_2:=A_{t_0}^{{\bf v}_2}L_2\in\mathcal U.$$ By $M=\frac{P_M}{A_{t_0}^{\bf d}}=\frac{L_1L_2}{A_{t_0}^{\bf d}}=\frac{U_1U_2}{A_{t_0}^{{\bf d}+{\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2}}$, we get
\begin{eqnarray} MA_{t_0}^{{\bf d}+{\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2}=U_1U_2,
\end{eqnarray}
which is an equality in $\mathcal U$, since ${\bf d},{\bf v}_1,{\bf v}_2\in\mathbb N^n$. Because $\mathcal U$ is factorial and $M$ is irreducible in $\mathcal U$, we get that either $U_1$ or $U_2$ is divisible by $M$ in $\mathcal U$. Without loss of generality, we assume that $U_1^\prime:=U_1/M\in\mathcal U$. Then by the equality (\ref{eqnmau}), we get $U_1^\prime U_2=A_{t_0}^{{\bf d}+{\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2},$ which implies that both $U_1^\prime$ and $U_2$ are invertible in $\mathcal L(t_0)$. So $L_2=U_2/A_{t_0}^{{\bf v}_2}$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_0)$. Hence,  $P_M$ is irreducible in $\mathcal L(t_0)$.

Since $P_M$ is irreducible in $\mathcal L(t_0)$ and by
the fact that $P_M$ is not divisible by any $Z_i$ and $A_{j;t_0}$ in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}],$ we get that $P_M$ is irreducible in $\mathbb K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_m][A_{1;t_0},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}]$. This completes the proof.

nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal U$ be the  geometric upper cluster algebra with initial extended exchange matrix $$\widetilde B_{t_0}= B_{t_0}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\3&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
We know that $\mathcal U$ is a full rank cluster algebra.  It is non-factorial, by Remark \ref{rmknonfactorial}. From the viewpoint of Theorem \ref{thmcufd}, the non-factoriality of $\mathcal U$ is due to the fact that the first exchange binomial $A_{2;t_0}^3+1=(A_{2;t_0}+1)(A_{2;t_0}^2-A_{2;t_0}+1)$ of $t_0$ is not irreducible.
nodes.section: 4.4 Examples of non-factorial upper cluster algebras
nodes.statement_short: For B=(0,-1;3,0), U is full rank but not factorial since A^3+1 factors.

nodes.name: Primitive but not factorial example
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a geometric cluster algebra with the following initial extended exchange matrix $$\widetilde B_{t_0}= B_{t_0}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ It is easy to see that $\widetilde B_{t_0}$ is primitive and acyclic but not full rank. It is known from \cite[Proposition 6.1]{GLS13} that $\mathcal A$ is not factorial. Since $\mathcal A$ is acyclic, $\mathcal A$ coincides with its upper cluster algebra $\mathcal U$, by Proposition \ref{proacyclic}. So $\mathcal U=\mathcal A$ is not factorial.
nodes.section: 4.4 Examples of non-factorial upper cluster algebras
nodes.statement_short: An acyclic primitive (non full rank) 3x3 example whose (upper) cluster algebra is not factorial.

nodes.name: Factorial cluster algebras are intersections of two Laurent rings
nodes.statement: {\rm (}\cite[Corollary 4.2]{GLS13}{\rm ).} Let $\mathcal A$ be a geometric cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and $\mathcal U$ its upper cluster algebra. Let $t, t_0$ be two seeds of $\mathcal A$ with no common cluster variables. If $\mathcal A$ is factorial, then $$\mathcal A=\mathcal U=\mathcal L(t)\cap\mathcal L(t_0),$$ where $\mathcal L(t)=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t}^{\pm1}]$ and $\mathcal L(t_0)=\mathbb {KP}[A_{1;t_0}^{\pm1},\ldots,A_{n;t_0}^{\pm1}]$.

assumptions: Let $\mathcal A$ be a geometric cluster algebra with coefficient semifield  $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$  and $\mathcal U$ its upper cluster algebra.
Let $t, t_0$ be two seeds of $\mathcal A$ with no common cluster variables.
$\mathcal A$ is factorial

nodes.name: Factorial cluster algebras equal upper cluster algebras
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{proglsau}, a factorial geometric cluster algebra must coincide with its upper cluster algebra. This provides a reason why we focus on the factoriality of upper cluster algebras rather than cluster algebras.

nodes.name: A=U iff A factorial for full rank primitive
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank, primitive upper cluster algebra and $\mathcal A$ the corresponding cluster algebra. Then $\mathcal A=\mathcal U$ if and only if $\mathcal A$ is factorial.

assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be a full rank, primitive upper cluster algebra and $\mathcal A$ the corresponding cluster algebra.
conclusions: $\mathcal A=\mathcal U$ if and only if $\mathcal A$ is factorial

nodes.name: Associate cluster variables are equal
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be a geometric upper cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and $A_{i;t_0}, A_{j;t}$ two cluster variables of $\mathcal U$. Then $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ are associate in $\mathcal U$ if and only if $A_{i;t_0}=A_{j;t}$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Ray Fish Theorem
assumptions: Let $\mathcal U$ be a geometric upper cluster algebra with coefficient semifield $\mathbb P={\rm Trop}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ and $A_{i;t_0}, A_{j;t}$ two cluster variables of $\mathcal U$.
conclusions: $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ are associate in $\mathcal U$ if and only if $A_{i;t_0}=A_{j;t}$
nodes.label: lemassociate

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.22
nodes.statement: Assume that $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ are associate in $\mathcal U$. Then \begin{eqnarray} A_{j;t}=\lambda Z_1^{c_1}\cdots Z_m^{c_m}A_{i;t_0} \end{eqnarray} for some $\lambda\in\mathbb K^\times$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in \mathbb Z$, by Theorem \ref{thmgls} (ii). Notice that the equality (\ref{eqnassociate}) can be viewed as the Laurent expansion of $A_{j;t}$ with respect to $t_0$. It is easy to see that $(A_{i;t_0}\mid\mid A_{j;t})_d=-1$. Then by Proposition \ref{rmkdf} (4), we get $A_{j;t}=A_{i;t_0}$. Conversely, assume $A_{i;t_0}=A_{j;t}$. Clearly, we have that $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ are associate in $\mathcal U$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 4.5 Ray Fish Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Associates differ by a unit, so the d-compatibility degree is -1 and Proposition 2.30 (4) gives equality.

nodes.name: Associate implies equal

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume $A_{i;t_0}=A_{j;t}$. Clearly, we have that   $A_{i;t_0}$ and $A_{j;t}$ are associate in $\mathcal U$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial direction.
