nodes.name: Length function lambda
nodes.statement:
Let 
 \begin{eqnarray} \lambda:\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\} \rightarrow \mathbb N \nonumber
 \end{eqnarray}
 be the map defined by $\lambda(M):=\sum_{j=0}^n\lambda_{t_j}(M)$, where $M\in \widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\}$.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Domain of lambda
nodes.statement: \lambda:\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\} \rightarrow \mathbb N \nonumber
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.label: eqn:lambda

nodes.name: Properties of lambda
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item [(i)] $\lambda(M)=0$ if and only if $M$ is invertible in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$. \item [(ii)] $\lambda(M\cdot N)=\lambda(M)+\lambda(N)$ for any $M,N\in\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
conclusions: $\lambda(M)=0$ if and only if $M$ is invertible in  $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$.
nodes.label: lem:app3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement: (i) Since $\lambda(M)=\sum_{j=0}^n \lambda_{t_j}(M)$ and each $\lambda_{t_j}(M)$ takes non-negative values, we know that $\lambda(M)=0$ if and only if $\lambda_{t_j}(M)=0$ for any $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem:app1} (i), we know that $\lambda_{t_j}(M)=0$ for any $j$ if and only if $M$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_j,{\bf inv})$ for any $j$. This happens if and only if $M$ is invertible in $\bigcap_{j=0}^n\mathcal L(t_j,{\bf inv})=\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$. (ii) This follows from Lemma \ref{lem:app1} (ii).
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Sum of nonnegative lambda_{t_j}; apply Lemma A.1 seed by seed.

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: (i) Since $\lambda(M)=\sum_{j=0}^n \lambda_{t_j}(M)$ and each $\lambda_{t_j}(M)$ takes non-negative values, we know that $\lambda(M)=0$ if and only if $\lambda_{t_j}(M)=0$ for any $j$. By Lemma \ref{lem:app1} (i), we know that $\lambda_{t_j}(M)=0$ for any $j$ if and only if $M$ is invertible in $\mathcal L(t_j,{\bf inv})$ for any $j$. This happens if and only if $M$ is invertible in $\bigcap_{j=0}^n\mathcal L(t_j,{\bf inv})=\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing iff invertible in every L(t_j,inv).
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement: (ii) This follows from Lemma \ref{lem:app1} (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Additivity of each lambda_{t_j}.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Atomicity via the length function
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a non-zero subring of $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$. Suppose whenever an element $r\in R$ is invertible in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$, it is invertible in $R$. Then $R$ is atomic. In particular, $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$ itself is atomic.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
assumptions: Let $R$ be a non-zero subring of $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$.
Suppose whenever an element $r\in R$ is invertible in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$, it is invertible in $R$.
conclusions: In particular, $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$ itself is atomic.
nodes.label: lem:app4

nodes.name: Length-function argument for Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: Indeed, the function $\lambda$ is a very special case of \emph{length function} on $R$ in the sense of \cite[Definition 1.1.3]{geroldinger2006non}, and the atomicity of $R$ is implied by \cite[Proposition 1.1.4]{geroldinger2006non}.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement_short: lambda is a length function, so atomicity follows from Geroldinger-Halter-Koch, Proposition 1.1.4.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: Fix a non-zero, non-invertible element $r\in R$. We need to show that it can be decomposed as a product of irreducible elements in $R$. Let $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ be a decomposition of $r$ such that each $a_i$ is a non-invertible element in $R\setminus\{0\}$. Such a decomposition exists, because we can always take $s=1$ and $a_1=r$. Fix a decomposition $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ as above. This decomposition can be viewed as decomposition in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\}$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:app3} (ii), we have $$\lambda(r)=\lambda(a_1)+\ldots +\lambda(a_s).$$ Since each $a_i$ is not invertible in $R$ and, by the assumption, we know that it is also not invertible in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:app3} (i), we have $\lambda(a_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 1}$. Hence, \begin{eqnarray} \lambda(r)=\lambda(a_1)+\ldots +\lambda(a_s)\geq s.\nonumber \end{eqnarray} Since $s$ is bounded by $\lambda(r)$, there exists a decomposition $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ such that $s$ is maximal. We claim that in such a decomposition, each $a_i$ is irreducible in $R$. Otherwise, there exists some $i_0$ such that $a_{i_0}$ is not irreducible in $R$. Without loss of generality, we can assume $i_0=s$. Then there exist two non-invertible elements $a_s',a_s''$ in $R\setminus\{0\}$ such that $a_s=a_s'a_s''$. Thus we have $$r=a_1\cdots a_{s-1}a_s'a_s'',$$ which is a decomposition of $r$ of length $s+1$ satisfying that each factor is not invertible in $R\setminus\{0\}$. This contradicts the choice of $s$. Hence, $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ is a decomposition of $r\in R$ satisfying that each $a_i$ is irreducible in $R$. Therefore, $R$ is atomic.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Decompositions into non-units have length at most lambda(r); a maximal-length decomposition consists of irreducibles.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Fix a non-zero, non-invertible element $r\in R$. We need to show that it can be decomposed as a product of irreducible elements in $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix r and aim for an irreducible decomposition.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Decompositions exist
nodes.statement: Let $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ be a decomposition of $r$ such that each $a_i$ is a non-invertible element in $R\setminus\{0\}$. Such a decomposition exists, because we can always take $s=1$ and $a_1=r$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompositions into non-units exist (s=1).
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Length bound
nodes.statement:
Fix a decomposition $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ as above. This decomposition can be viewed as decomposition in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})\setminus\{0\}$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:app3} (ii), we have $$\lambda(r)=\lambda(a_1)+\ldots +\lambda(a_s).$$
Since each $a_i$ is not invertible in $R$ and, by the assumption, we know that it is also not invertible in $\widetilde {\mathcal U}({\bf inv})$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:app3} (i), we have $\lambda(a_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 1}$.
Hence, 
\begin{eqnarray} \lambda(r)=\lambda(a_1)+\ldots +\lambda(a_s)\geq s.\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma A.3 gives lambda(r) >= s.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Maximal decomposition
nodes.statement: Since $s$ is bounded by $\lambda(r)$, there exists a decomposition $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ such that $s$ is maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a decomposition of maximal length.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Claim: factors irreducible
nodes.statement:
We claim that in such a decomposition, each $a_i$ is irreducible in $R$. Otherwise, 
there exists some $i_0$ such that $a_{i_0}$ is not irreducible in $R$. Without loss of generality, we can assume $i_0=s$.
Then there exist two non-invertible elements $a_s',a_s''$ in $R\setminus\{0\}$ such that $a_s=a_s'a_s''$. Thus we have $$r=a_1\cdots a_{s-1}a_s'a_s'',$$ which is a decomposition of $r$ of length $s+1$ satisfying that each factor is not invertible in $R\setminus\{0\}$. This contradicts the choice of $s$. Hence,  $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ is a decomposition of $r\in R$ satisfying that each $a_i$ is irreducible in $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximality forces irreducible factors.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Assume reducible factor
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, 
there exists some $i_0$ such that $a_{i_0}$ is not irreducible in $R$. Without loss of generality, we can assume $i_0=s$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose a_s is reducible.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Longer decomposition
nodes.statement: Then there exist two non-invertible elements $a_s',a_s''$ in $R\setminus\{0\}$ such that $a_s=a_s'a_s''$. Thus we have $$r=a_1\cdots a_{s-1}a_s'a_s'',$$ which is a decomposition of $r$ of length $s+1$ satisfying that each factor is not invertible in $R\setminus\{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting a_s gives length s+1.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: This contradicts the choice of $s$. Hence,  $r=a_1\cdots a_s$ is a decomposition of $r\in R$ satisfying that each $a_i$ is irreducible in $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradicts maximality.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, $R$ is atomic.
nodes.statement_short: R is atomic.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3

nodes.name: Length bound lambda(r) >= s
nodes.statement: \lambda(r)=\lambda(a_1)+\ldots +\lambda(a_s)\geq s.\nonumber

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: Thanks to Lemma \ref{lem:app2}, we can apply Lemma \ref{lem:app4} to the case $R=\mathcal U({\bf inv})$ or $R=\mathcal A({\bf inv})$. Hence, $\mathcal U({\bf inv})$ and $\mathcal A({\bf inv})$ are atomic.
nodes.section: Appendix: The proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma A.4 to U(inv) and A(inv), using the unit description of Lemma A.2.
